==Problem 16 ==

Minh enters the numbers <imath>1</imath> through <imath>81</imath> into the cells of a <imath>9 \times 9</imath> grid in some order. She calculates the product of the numbers in each row and column. What is the least number of rows and columns that could have a product divisible by <imath>3</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 8\qquad\textbf{(B) } 9\qquad\textbf{(C) } 10\qquad\textbf{(D) } 11\qquad\textbf{(E) } 12</imath>

==Solution 1==
Note you can swap/rotate any configuration of rows, such that all the rows and columns that have a product of 3 are in the top left. Hence the points are bounded by a <imath>a \times b</imath> rectangle. This has <imath>ab</imath> area and <imath>a+b</imath> rows and columns divisible by <imath>3</imath>. We want <imath>ab\ge 27</imath> and <imath>a+b</imath> minimized. 

If <imath>ab=27</imath>, we achieve minimum with <imath>a+b=9+3=12</imath>.

If <imath>ab=28</imath>,our best is <imath>a+b=7+4=11</imath>. Note if <imath>a+b=10</imath>, <imath>ab=25</imath>. Because <imath>25<27</imath>, there is no smaller answer, and we get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)} 11}</imath>.

==Solution 2==
For a row or column to have a product divisible by <imath>3</imath>, there must be a multiple of <imath>3</imath> in the row or column. To create the least amount of rows and columns with multiples of <imath>3</imath>, we must find a way to keep them all together, to minimize the total number of rows and columns with multiples of threes in it. From <imath>1</imath> to <imath>81</imath>, there are <imath>27</imath> multiples of <imath>3</imath> <imath>(81/3 = 27)</imath>. So we have to fill <imath>27</imath> cells with numbers that are multiples of <imath>3</imath>. If we put <imath>25</imath> of these numbers in a <imath>5 * 5</imath> grid, there would be <imath>5</imath> rows and <imath>5</imath> columns (<imath>10</imath> in total), with products divisible by <imath>3</imath>. However, we have <imath>27</imath> numbers, so <imath>2</imath> numbers still need to be put in the <imath>9 * 9</imath> grid. If we put both numbers in the <imath>6</imath>th column, but one in the first row, and one in the second row, (next to the <imath>5</imath> by <imath>5</imath> grid already filled), we would have a total of <imath>6</imath> columns now, and still <imath>5</imath> rows with products that are multiples of <imath>3</imath>. Since <imath>6 + 5 = 11</imath>, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)} 11}</imath>

==Solution 3==

In the numbers <imath>1</imath> to <imath>81</imath>, there are 27 multiples of three. In order to minimize the rows and columns, the best way is to make a square. However, the closest square is <imath>25</imath>, meaning there are two multiples of three remaining. However, you can place these multiples right above the 5x5 square, meaning the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf {(D)} 11}</imath>
